As of 326 PM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall 
is expected tonight through Friday, with a few thunderstorms 
possible.


Afternoon weather analysis shows a broad upper trough extending over 
the eastern 2/3 of the United States with the stronger flow centered 
over the Ohio River valley. While at the surface, a sub-1000mb low 
sits over northern Canada while its associated cold front drags all 
the way down the spine of the Appalachians, while to the east high 
pressure sits off the coast. With the cold front slowly pushing east 
it is allowing the high pressure to continue to filter in a warm and 
humid airmass for this time of year  across the local area. Cloud 
cover was able to clear out across the SE and Eastern Shore allowing 
for temperatures to rise into the upper 70s to low 80s. While across 
the Piedmont cloud cover and light showers have been able to persist 
through much of the day causing temps to reach into the low 70s.  

By this evening the cold front is expected to move into the area 
before stalling once again. The cold front is likely to stall along 
the I-85 corridor allowing for showers and a possible thunderstorm 
to track along the boundary. The environment ahead of the boundary is 
favorable for heavy rainfall as weak instability and PWATS over 200+ 
percent of normal for early November is forecasted to be in place. 
Confidence is increasing that the Middle Peninsula and eastern 
Northern Neck, up to the Maryland Eastern Shore is likely to see 
moderate to heavy rainfall as the CAMS and ensembles come into 
better agreement. Some of the areas are likely to see 1-2" with 
higher totals associated with the higher precip late tonight/early 
tomorrow morning. While across the piedmont and and up into the RIC 
metro areas may receive upwards of 1" as weaker forcing will likely 
be in place. Friday morning and into Friday afternoon, a wave of low 
pressure is forecasted to move out of the NW helping to advance the 
cold front through the area and pushing the showers and isolated 
storms east. The environment will be very similar with perhaps some 
higher instability across the southeast and stronger upper level 
forcing. Withe the stronger upper level forcing this may 
potentially allow for more storm development. The shear vectors do 
support possible training of storms which may potentially lead to 
very localized flash flooding. The REFS ensemble looks to be the 
most reasonable with 1-2"+inches likely across SE VA and NE NC with 
possible 3"+ with any training storms. Will note that the HRRR and 
RRFS look to be very aggressive with widespread storm development 
leading to much higher totals. In addition to the possible flash 
flooding threat, there is also a very marginal severe threat across 
the south. Bulk-Shear will generally remain between 35-45kt and a ML-
CAPE reaching near 500J/kg. These ingredients together could allow 
for a brief strong wind gusts with any stronger storm embedded in 
the line of showers/isolated storms tomorrow. There is also a very 
small tornado threat due to the weak 0-1 SRH (~100m^2/s^2), however, 
confidence is low at this time. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drying out and becoming seasonably cool this 
weekend into early next week. 

The chances of rain diminish by late Friday afternoon as the stronger 
cold front advances through the area. A closed low pressure will 
drop out of the NW and into the northern Mid- Atlantic/southern New 
England region on Saturday, reinforcing our northwesterly flow. Much 
cooler and drier air is forecasted to advect into the area, 
dropping high temps back to seasonable. Highs this weekend and 
into early next week will generally be in the mid to upper 60s. 
Winds Saturday will be breezy as wind gusts will be around 
20-25mph out of the NW. Overnight lows will drop into the mid to
upper 30s (low 40s by the coast) each night. The recent 
ensembles are continuing to show dry weather persisting into the
middle of next week as opposed to bringing in any more rain 
chances.
